Title: CT-based skeletal muscle loss predicts long term prognosis in patients with distal cholangiocarcinoma undergone pancreaticoduodenectomy
Text:
CT-based skeletal muscle loss 
predicts long term prognosis 
in patients with distal 
cholangiocarcinoma undergone 
pancreaticoduodenectomy
Guangzhen Qu1, Shao-Cheng Lyu2, Yong Zhang1, Kun Gao1 & Chuanguo Zhou1
Skeletal muscle index (SMI), as an effective indicator of nutritional status, plays an important role in 
the prognosis of malignancy. However, the impact of skeletal muscle changes on tumor prognosis has 
not been systematically elaborated. We aimed to explore the value of skeletal muscle changes in the 
prognosis of distal cholangiocarcinoma (DCC) patients undergone pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD). 
Patients who underwent PD for DCC between 2015 and 2023 were included in this study. Demographic, 
laboratory and follow-up information was obtained. The cross-sectional images of skeletal muscle area 
at the level of the third lumbar spine was obtained based on computed tomography (CT), and the SMI 
was calculated by skeletal muscle mass through height squared normalization. Skeletal muscle index 
and skeletal muscle loss (SML) were obtained before PD and three to six months after surgery. Patients 
were classified into two groups (High-SML and Low-SML) based on the optimal SML cut-off value. The 
univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards analysis was conducted to evaluate the influence 
of SML in predicting over survival (OS) and recurrence free survival (RFS) of DCC. Of the 112 patients 
with distal cholangiocarcinoma, 55 (49%) were diagnosed with low SMI preoperatively. The best cut-off 
values of SML were − 4.01% and − 5.99% for OS and RFS. In multivariate analysis, tumor size  > 2.0 cm 
(hazard ratio (HR) = 1.90, P = 0.017), poor differentiation (hazard ratio (HR) = 2.80, P > 0.001), higher 
SML (SML ≤ − 4.01%) (hazard ratio (HR) = 3.60, P  < 0.001), lymph metastasis (hazard ratio (HR) = 4.00, 
P  < 0.001) and vascular invasion (hazard ratio (HR) = 2.10, P  = 0.013) were independent risk factors 
forOS. Meanwhile, poor differentiation (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.90, P = 0.043), higher SML (SML ≤ -5.99%) 
(hazard ratio (HR) = 3.80, P < 0.001) and lymph metastasis (hazard ratio (HR) = 2.60, P = 0.003) was an 
independent risk factor forRFS. The models combining SML and clinical characteristics had excellent 
predictive performance for OS and RFS. The nutritional status marker SML are effective and convenient 
indicators for predicting the long-term prognosis of DCC after PD, and the SMLafter PD is notable. 
The combination of CT quantified SML and clinical features can help clinicians predict the long-term 
survival of DCC patients after PD.
Keywords  Distal cholangiocarcinoma, Pancreaticoduodenectomy, Skeletal muscle index, Skeletal muscle 
loss, Overall survival, Recurrence free survival
Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is a highly lethal and heterogeneous malignancy, according to anatomical position, 
it can be categorized into intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA) and 
the distal bile duct carcinoma (dCCA)1,2. Originating from the common bile duct, distal cholangiocarcinoma 
is a type of cancer found below the gallbladder and hepatic duct junction and above the ampulla of Vater, 
comprising 20-30% of all cholangiocarcinomas3,4. Patients with distal cholangiocarcinoma typically present with 
painless jaundice as a result of biliary obstruction, prompting them to seek medical evaluation. Laboratory tests 
frequently demonstrate elevated levels of bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, G-glutamyl transpeptidase, and liver 
transaminase. EUS-FNA (Endoscopic ultrasonic fine needle aspiration) exhibits higher sensitivity in detecting

dCCA5. In terms of therapy, the complex tumor microenvironment and presence of genetic heterogeneity 
may pose an obstacle to the delivery of chemotherapy drugs to the malignancy6. Surgical intervention, 
particularly through procedures like PD or Whipple surgery, is seen as the most effective treatment for early 
and mid-stage distal cholangiocarcinoma. However, the long-term survival outcomes following PD for distal 
cholangiocarcinoma remain suboptimal6,7. For patients with advanced cholangiocarcinoma who cannot undergo 
surgery or locoregional treatments, the main treatment strategy involves chemotherapy with gemcitabine and 
cisplatin8. Studies have indicated that the combination regimen confers a modest survival advantage compared 
to gemcitabine monotherapy, with median survival durations of 8.1 months and 11.7 months, respectively9. In 
recent years, immunotherapy has become a crucial treatment option for different advanced cancers, including 
both solid and non-solid tumors. Immunotherapy has demonstrated efficacy in tumors exhibiting mismatch 
repair defects (dMMR), high microsatellite instability (MSI), or high tumor mutation load (hTMB)10,11. 
Regrettably, cholangiocarcinoma, particularly advanced cholangiocarcinoma, frequently lacks these 
distinguishing features. Nevertheless, proof exists that CCA is immunogenic, which supports the argument for 
further study of immunotherapy, both as a standalone treatment and in combination with other therapies12–15.
Malnutrition has been linked to decreased survival rates and diminished quality of life among patients with 
various types of cancer16,17. According to research, around 70% of patients with malignant tumors in hospitals are 
malnourished, and malnutrition is a factor in the deaths of approximately 20% of cancer patients18,19. Currently, 
sarcopenia, as assessed by SMI derived from radiological images, has emerged as a critical parameter in the 
clinical assessment of nutritional status and prognostication for patients with tumors. Sarcopenia is typified by a 
reduction in skeletal muscle mass and strength and is observed across various conditions including liver, kidney, 
inflammatory diseases, and malignancies20. Sarcopenia serves as an adverse prognostic factor in cancer patients, 
whereas preservation of muscle mass may potentially extend survival in this population21,22. A meta-analysis by 
Liu et al.23 revealed that preoperative sarcopenia was independently associated with OS (HR = 1.53, P < 0.00001) 
and progression-free survival (HR = 1.55, P < 0.00001). Findings reveal that preoperative sarcopenia is linked 
to a higher rate of postoperative complications in esophageal cancer patients and is an independent factor 
affecting their long-term prognosis24,25. In terms of non-solid tumor, it has been shown that decreased SMI is 
an independent risk factor for OS and RFS in diffuse large B-cell lymphomas26. Marasco et al.27 showed that 
low SMI or sarcopenia was positively associated with poor prognosis in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma 
who underwent partial hepatectomy or systemic therapy. According to these studies, low SMI or sarcopenia 
may affect the long-term prognosis of patients with malignant tumors following surgery or systemic treatment. 
However, there is a shortage of long-term data on the prognosis of DCC patients who have undergone PD with 
low SMI, dynamic skeletal muscle loss, and inflammatory status. The objective of this study was to evaluate 
the effects of pre- and post-surgical SMI alterations on the outcomes of distal cholangiocarcinoma patients 
undergoing PD.
Materials and methods
Research design
This retrospective, single-centre study collected information of distal cholangiocarcinoma patients who underwent 
PD in our hospital from July 2015 to June 2023. Inclusion criteria include: (1) Distal cholangiocarcinoma 
patients undergoing PD, (2) Absence of neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy before surgery, (3) No 
deaths occurring in the perioperative period. Following this, patients were excluded based on these criteria: (1) 
Presence of other tumors before surgery, (2) Receipt of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, (3) Lack of complete data 
during the perioperative period. Patient group selection is represented by a flowchart (Fig. 1).
Data collection and follow-up
Demographic and clinical variables was retrospectively collected from the electronic medical record system. 
These indicators include: age, gender, body mass index (BMI), American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA), 
presence of hypertension and diabetes, preoperative venous routine blood sample test, coagulation function, 
tumor markers, biochemical examination, tumor size, differentiation, and adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery. 
NLR was defined as the ratios of neutrophil count to lymphocyte count. To calculate SII, multiply the platelet 
count by the neutrophil count and divide by the lymphocyte count; for SIRI, multiply the monocyte count by the 
neutrophil count and divide by the lymphocyte count (monocyte count * neutrophil count/lymphocyte count). 
Patients underwent monitoring after being discharged, with check-ups every three months until December 2023 
or their death. The postoperative follow-up consisted of abdominal CT scans, blood routine tests, and biochemical 
evaluations. The initial detection of any new lesion suspected to be a recurrence following surgery was termed 
postoperative recurrence, encompassing areas such as the liver, pancreas, peritoneal lymph nodes, omentum, 
gastrointestinal tract, lung, bone, brain, etc., and the clinical diagnosis was made through the combination of CT 
and MRI, or pathological diagnosis was made when necessary. PD to death or last observation was defined as 
overall survival (OS), and PD to recurrence was defined as recurrence-free survival (RFS).
Skeletal muscle loss (SML) calculation by image analysis
The skeletal muscle area (SMA) of DCC before surgery based on CT cross-sectional images at the third lumbar 
vertebra level (L3) was measured using Slice-O-Matic V5.0 (TomoVision, Montreal, QC, Canada) software. 
Automatic segmentation of the skeletal muscles, including the psoas major, erector spinalis, quadratus psoas, 
transverse abdominis, and both internal and external obliques along with the rectus abdominis, was achieved 
using thresholds set between − 29 and 150 Hounsfield units (HU) (Fig. 2)28. Two radiologists, with 5 and 7 years of 
experience in imaging respectively, were invited to independently analyze the digital imaging data while blinded 
to patient information. The L3 skeletal muscle area (cm2) was measured and normalized by height squared to 
calculate the skeletal muscle index (SMI) for each patient, expressed in cm2/m2. According to according to

working group for creation of sarcopenia assessment criteria of Japan Society of Hepatology, sarcopenia was 
defined as SMI ≤ 42 cm2/m2 in men and ≤ 38 cm2/m2 in women29. The follow-up plan for patients after discharge 
includes outpatient visits every 1 to 2 months, which involve CT imaging and serum biochemical tests. The SMI 
value will be obtained within 3–6 months post-surgery. The SML=[(postoperative SMI - preoperative SMI)/
preoperative SMI × 100%]. All the information of patients was confidential, all patients signed informed consent, 
and this retrospective study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Statistical analysis
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was employed to assess the distribution of continuous data. Continuous 
variables following a normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation and analyzed using the 
independent samples t-test. For non-normally distributed data, variables were presented as median (interquartile 
range) and compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. The categorical variables were analyzed as percentages 
and compared using Pearson’s chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. The optimal cut-off values for SML and 
inflammation biomarkers according to the Youden index related to the endpoints such as OS and RFS was 
determined through receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curve analysis using R software. Univariate and 
multivariate Cox regression models were utilized to identify independent prognostic factors associated with OS 
and RFS. Variables with a significance level of P < 0.05 in the univariate Cox regression analysis were included 
in the multivariate Cox regression model. Survival differences were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier curves 
and compared with log-rank tests. All analyses were conducted using R (version 4.1.2), and P-value < 0.05 is 
considered statistically significant.
Results
Patient characteristics
A total of 112 patients meeting the inclusion criteria were enrolled in the study and categorized into low-SMI 
and high-SMI groups, comprising 55 and 57 patients, respectively (Table 1). The mean age of the cohort was 
64.89 ± 10.74 years, with 70 males (62%) and 42 females (38%). Baseline characteristics, including age, gender,

BMI, ASA classification, and the prevalence of hypertension and diabetes, showed no significant differences 
between the low-SMI and high-SMI groups. Similarly, no statistical differences were observed for preoperative 
leukocyte, neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, and platelet counts; prothrombin time (PT); international 
normalized ratio (INR); albumin; creatinine; intraoperative blood loss; adjuvant chemotherapy; NLR; SII; or SIRI 
(P > 0.05 for all comparisons). Notably, CA199 (median 61.92 versus 43.91, P = 0.041), total bilirubin (median 
184.60 versus 107.00, P = 0.006), SML (median − 2.85 versus − 1.55, P < 0.001) and SML% (mean − 7.96% versus 
− 3%, P < 0.001) were significantly elevated in low SMI group, and the difference was remarkable. The mean 
SMI were 36.9 ± 4.52 and 45.25 ± 5.25 in low-SMI group and high-SMI group, respectively. In the pathological 
information, there was no discrepancy in tumor size and vascular invasion between the two groups (P > 0.05). 
Notably, the proportion of lymph node metastasis was significantly higher in the low-SMI group compared to 
the high-SMI group (60% versus 25%, P = 0.001). The proportion of poor differentiation was higher in low SMI 
group, compared with high SMI group (45% versus 25%, P = 0.002). Concerning tumor recurrence, 49 cases 
(44%) recurred, with 25 cases and 24 cases in high SMI and low SMI groups, respectively (P = 0.9) (Table 2). 
Among the patients, there were 39 cases of liver metastasis, 15 cases of abdominal lymph node metastasis, 4 cases 
of adrenal gland metastasis, 6 cases involving the brain, lung, and bone, 5 cases affecting the pancreas, colon, and 
stomach, and 7 cases with metastases in other locations. Notably, some patients with distal cholangiocarcinoma 
(DCC) presented with multiple simultaneous metastatic sites.
The impact of SML and inflammatory markers on OS and RFS
The changes in SMI were evaluated in patients with DCC before surgery and 3–6 months postoperatively. 
Overall, SMI exhibited a significant decline post-surgery compared to preoperative levels (39.02 ± 7.01 versus 
41.27 ± 5.94, P < 0.001). This downward trend was observed in both the low-SMI group (34.15 ± 4.41 versus 
37.39 ± 4.11, P < 0.001) and the high-SMI group (43.72 ± 5.74 versus 45.02 ± 4.94, P < 0.001). These findings are 
visually represented in the box plot (Supplementary Fig. 1). Additionally, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) 
curves were utilized to investigate the relationship between SML, preoperative inflammatory biomarkers, and 
postoperative long-term outcomes following PD surgery. The R software was utilized to determine the optimal 
cut-off values for the prognostic markers SML, NLR, SII, and SIRI in patients with DCC following PD surgery. 
The cut-off values for OS established for these markers were − 4.01%, 2.17, 505.05 and 1.48, respectively. Patients 
were stratified into two groups based on these cut-off values: a high SML and inflammatory markers group, and 
a low SML and inflammatory markers group.
Kaplan-Meier curve analysis with log-rank tests was performed to evaluate overall survival (OS) differences 
among groups stratified by skeletal muscle loss (SML) and inflammatory biomarkers. Patients in the high SML 
group (SML ≤ -4.01%) demonstrated significantly poorer prognoses compared to those in the low SML group 
(SML > -4.01%), with P < 0.001 (Fig. 3A). Similarly, analysis of inflammatory biomarkers revealed that patients 
in the high NLR (P = 0.017), SII (P = 0.012), and SIRI (P = 0.002) groups had markedly worse OS compared to 
those with lower values of these markers (Fig. 3B–D).
Similarly, R software was used to determine the optimal cut-off value of prognostic indicators SML, NLR, 
SII, and SIRI for RFS after PD in DCC patients. The cut-off values for RFS established for these markers were 
− 5.99%, 2.26, 469.01 and 1.35, respectively. The study utilized Kaplan-Meier curves with log rank t-tests to 
assess prognostic differences among various groups of related prognostic markers. Results indicated that the

Clinical characteristics analysis of patients in different SML groups
As shown in Table 3, the 112 DCC patients were divided into low SML (N = 46) and high SML (N = 66) groups 
based on the cut-off value of SML for overall survival (OS). Notably, the high SML group exhibited significantly 
higher levels of leukocytes (mean 7.26 vs. 6.22, P = 0.004), neutrophils (mean 4.94 vs. 4.20, P = 0.004), monocytes 
(mean 0.51 vs. 0.42, P = 0.015), SII (median 837.28 vs. 775.35, P = 0.042), and SIRI (median 1.70 vs. 1.38, 
P < 0.001) compared to the low SML group. In terms of clinicopathological features, compared with low SML 
group, high SML group had a higher proportion of poor differentiation (45% versus 20%, P = 0.005) and lymph 
metastasis (55% versus 24%, P = 0.001) (Table 3).

Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analysis for OS
Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were performed to identify factors influencing overall 
survival (OS) following pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) in patients with DCC. Univariate Cox regression analysis 
revealed that the following factors were associated with poorer OS: CA199 > 37 (HR = 1.74, 95% CI, 1.02–2.95, 
P = 0.041), tumor size > 2 cm (HR = 1.89, 95% CI, 1.15–3.09, P = 0.012), poor differentiation (HR = 3.04, 95% CI, 
1.84–5.03, P < 0.001), vascular invasion (invasion versus non-invasion, HR = 2.0, 95% CI, 1.1–3.6, P < 0.001), 
lymph node metastasis (HR = 4.23, 95% CI, 2.51–7.12, P < 0.001), and SML ≤ -4.01% (HR = 4.53, 95% CI, 2.56–
8.04, P < 0.001) (Table 4). These factors were identified as independent risk factors affecting OS in DCC patients. 
Variables with a P value < 0.05 in the univariate Cox regression analysis were included in the multivariate Cox 
regression analysis. Tumor diameter (> 2 cm) (HR = 1.90, (95% CI, 1.12–3.20), P = 0.017), poor differentiation 
(HR = 2.80, (95% CI, 1.57–4.90), P < 0.001), vascular invasion (HR = 2.10, (95% CI, 1.17–3.70), P = 0.013), lymph 
metastasis (HR = 4.00, (95% CI, 2.27–7.00), P < 0.001), and high SML (≤-4.01%) (HR = 3.60, (95% CI, 1.96–
6.80), P < 0.001) are identified as independent risk factors impacting OS in multivariate Cox regression analysis 
(Table 4).
Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analysis for RFS
Additionally, univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were performed to identify significant factors 
influencing RFS following PD for DCC. ROC curve analysis determined a critical threshold of -5.99% for 
SML as a predictor of RFS. Based on this cut-off value, patients were stratified into two groups. Univariate 
Cox regression analysis identified CA199 > 37 (HR = 2.25, (95% CI, 1.19–4.24), P = 0.013), poor differentiation 
(HR = 2.25, (95% CI, 1.26–4.02), P = 0.006), lymph metastasis (HR = 3.32, (95% CI, 1.81–6.08), P < 0.001) and 
SML (≤-5.99%) (HR = 4.50, (95% CI, 2.39–8.47), P < 0.001) as independent risk factors associated with RFS 
(Table 5). Multivariate Cox regression analysis showed that poor differentiation (HR = 1.90, (95% CI, 1.02–3.50), 
P = 0.043), lymph metastasis (HR = 2.6, (95% CI, 1.39–5.00), P = 0.003) and high SML (≤-5.99%) (HR = 3.80, 
(95% CI, 1.97–7.50), P < 0.001) were identified as independent risk factors for recurrence free survival (Table 5).

The ROC curve analyses demonstrated the predictive abilities of SML and clinical characteristics combinations

Therefore, it is necessary to develop imaging information and blood and biochemical indicators to evaluate the

Malnutrition has been linked to a poor prognosis in various types of tumors and is often a direct cause of 
death in patients with advanced-stage tumors. The SMI, derived from CT imaging data, is considered a more 
accurate indicator of nutritional status. The use of SMI to evaluate sarcopenia for predicting cancer patients’ 
long-term prognosis is gaining attention. In our retrospective study, we examined 112 patients with DCC who 
underwent PD. Of these patients, 55 (49%) were classified as low SMI and 57 (51%) as high SMI. Our findings 
suggest that dynamic changes in skeletal muscle index (i.e. SML) are effective predictors of OS and RFS.
Sarcopenia, assessed by the SMI at the third lumbar vertebra level on CT images, has been recognized as a 
significant prognostic factor in various malignancies. The use of CT imaging to quantify fat and muscle areas 
for prognostic assessment has emerged as a straightforward and accurate method. Jang et al.’s33. suggests that 
while using SMI as a static measurement is valid, applying it as a dynamic variable may be more appropriate for

leading to subsequent alterations in SMI. Therefore, in our study, we measured the SMI of patients with DCC 
measured by CT imaging data before PD and the SMI 3–6 months after PD, and predicted the long-term OS and 
RFS through the SML.
Multiple studies have demonstrated that among patients with hepatocellular carcinoma undergone 
hepatectomy, the prevalence of preoperative low SMI ranges from 14 to 40.3%34–37. This higher prevalence may 
be attributed to variations in tumor types and the presence of jaundice in certain patients, which can impact liver 
metabolism and the digestion and absorption functions of related organs, leading to persistent malnutrition. 
Within the low SMI group, levels of total bilirubin and CA199 were significantly elevated compared to those in 
the high SMI group. This shows that in the low SMI group, the proportion of patients with obstructive jaundice 
is slightly higher, and the continuously rising jaundice further affects liver function, even induces cholangitis and 
liver dysfunction, which will also promote the increase of CA199.
Our study aimed to assess changes in skeletal muscle and their impact on OS and RFS in patients with 
DCC. The optimal cut-off values for SML in relation to OS and RFS were determined to be -4.01% and − 5.99%, 
respectively. Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed a significant reduction in OS among patients with SML ≤ -4.01% 
compared to those with SML > -4.01%. Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified tumor diameter ≥ 2 cm, 
poor differentiation, vascular invasion, lymph node metastasis, and SML ≤ -4.01% as independent risk factors 
for decreased OS in DCC. In the analysis of factors affecting RFS after PD in DCC, poor differentiation, lymph 
metastasis and SML≤-5.99% were independent risk factors. Kuwada et al.38 demonstrated that SML serves as an 
independent risk prognostic factor impacting the OS of gastric cancer patients who have undergone gastrectomy 
(hazard ratio [HR] = 2.65; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.68–4.20, P < 0.0001). Furthermore, the 5-year RFS 
rate was significantly lower in the SML group compared to the non-SML group (73% versus 86%, P = 0.006 and 
56% versus 87%, P < 0.0001). In contrast to previous research, our study focuses on the specific reduction in SML 
value that influences the prognosis of DCC in the period before and after PD. By examining the specific SML 
value, patients with DCC can be categorized into various risk groups, allowing for personalized and preventive 
treatment approaches to improve outcomes. Yang et al.’s39 research demonstrated that in patients receiving 
adjuvant transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) following hepatectomy, SML<-2.42% serves as a significant 
predictor of decreased cause-specific survival (CSS). Our own investigation indicates that SML≤-4.01% and 
SML≤-5.99% are the most reliable indicators of shortened OS and RFS. The difference in specific values of

SML may be due to the difference in tumor types, and the effect of PD on the recovery of nutritional status and

Currently, SML is recognized as a prognostic indicator for individuals with malignancies, specifically cancer 
cachexia, which has been shown to substantially elevate mortality rates in cancer patients40. SML has been 
observed in patients with various types of tumors post-treatment, such as gastric cancer, liver cancer, non-small 
cell lung cancer, and pancreatic cancer41–44. Our findings align with previous studies, as evidenced by a mean SML 
of -5.81% in 112 DCC patients. PD entails the resection of multiple digestive organs and complex reconstruction 
of the digestive tract, which significantly impairs normal physiological functions. Partial pancreatic resection 
reduces pancreatic enzyme secretion, resulting in impaired digestion and absorption of proteins and fats. This 
disruption ultimately hinders patients’ long-term nutritional status and immune recovery. Additionally, complex 
reconstruction of the digestive tract postoperatively can result in gastrointestinal dysfunction, further impacting 
the nutritional and immune status of patients following surgery. This may be an important reason for the loss of 
skeletal muscle in most patients with DCC after PD. Therefore, early assessment of nutritional status in patients 
with DCC undergoing PD, coupled with timely nutritional intervention for those experiencing skeletal muscle 
loss, may contribute to improved overall nutritional outcomes.
Inflammatory biomarkers, such as NLR, SII and SIRI, are closely correlated to the prognosis of a variety of 
tumors, which has been confirmed in many studies45–48. There is a correlation between nutritional status and 
immune inflammatory response. Nutritional deficiency triggers the release of immune cells and inflammatory 
mediators, impairing patients’ immune surveillance and response functions. Our findings indicate that 
combining SML with the SIRI can improve risk stratification for patients with DCC after PD. This information 
is crucial for tailoring nutritional interventions for individual DCC patients, allowing for the development of 
personalized follow-up strategies based on specific risk profiles. Previous studies have indicated that excess body 
weight, specifically overweight or obesity, is a significant risk factor for the development of various malignancies 
and chronic conditions, ultimately impacting the long-term prognosis49. Individuals with cancer who exhibit 
reduced skeletal muscle mass and increased BMI are linked to less favorable long-term prognoses compared to 
those with greater muscle mass and lower BMI50. Baracos’s51 research showed that obese patients with sarcopenia 
exhibit diminished functional status and short-term and long-term prognosis than obese patients without 
sarcopenia. During our research, we categorized patients with DCC post-PD into two groups (BMI > 25 kg/m2

that we chose the dynamic combination of SMI, and there were few samples with high SML & BMI > 25 kg/m2. 
Therefore, a large sample size multicenter study should explore the value of SML combined with obesity in the 
long-term prognosis after surgery in malignancy.
An increasing body of research is investigating the impact of sarcopenia on tumor prognosis, alongside the 
development of associated clinical recommendations. However, limited attention has been directed toward the 
temporal variations in SMI during the perioperative period of malignancy, particularly pre- and post-surgery. 
Furthermore, the formulation of targeted intervention strategies based on these dynamic changes remains 
underexplored, presenting a critical gap in the current evidence base to guide clinical practice. CT is a reliable 
and efficient tool for evaluating muscle quality, offering numerous benefits. By utilizing CT to quantitatively 
assess SMI and SML in patients with DCC both pre- and post-operatively, one can effectively analyze long-term 
prognosis and risk stratification. Our study reveals a marked decline in skeletal muscle mass among patients 
with DCC undergoing surgery, which adversely affects OS and RFS. To counteract this trend, timely nutritional 
support interventions should be initiated postoperatively upon identifying SML. Additionally, the assessment of 
SML may assist in stratifying the prognostic risk of patients with DCC undergoing surgical intervention, as well 
as identifying individuals who may benefit from early nutritional and exercise interventions to enhance food 
intake, skeletal muscle quality and function, and mitigate preoperative inflammatory responses. The limitations 
of our study include its retrospective nature and being conducted at a single center, emphasizing the importance 
of future multi-center prospective studies for validation. Secondly, the SMI time interval measured by imaging 
in DCC patients with after PD is not consistent, which may have a certain degree of bias. Finally, although we 
dynamically measure the changes of SML, we also need to further measure the impact of dynamic changes of 
inflammatory biomarkers on DCC prognosis.
Conclusion
SML were identified as reliable independent prognostic factors for long-term overall survival and recurrence-
free survival in DCC patients undergone PD. The combination of SML and clinical features has superior 
performance in predicting the long-term prognosis of DCC. However, multicenter and extensive sample data 
are still needed to accurately evaluate the prognosis of patients with DCC, so as to provide more theoretical 
support for precise treatment.
